title: ARP and ping: the neighbours
summary: An IP address names a machine anywhere; a MAC address names the next box on the cable. ARP links the two, ping checks the machine answers.

text: On a local network, data travels in frames addressed to a network card, by its MAC address.
- ARP asks the whole local network "who has this IP?" and the owner answers with its MAC.
- Your machine keeps the answers for a while: ip neigh shows them (arp -a on a Mac).
- IPv6 does the same job with another protocol, neighbour discovery (NDP).
A far machine is not your neighbour: you never learn its MAC.
- The frame goes to your gateway's MAC (the router); the IP packet inside keeps the far address.
- Each router on the way unpacks it and sends it to its own next neighbour.
- So if ARP for the gateway fails, nothing outside your network works.

scheme: ping   ICMP, no port: is the machine there?
arping ARP: is it on my network? (Linux)
text: ping sends an ICMP echo request and waits for the echo reply: it tests the machine, not a service (ICMP has no port).
- No reply may be a firewall that drops ICMP, not a dead machine.
- On your own network, a machine that drops ping still answers ARP: sudo arping -c 3 192.168.1.20 shows it's there (Debian: apt install iputils-arping).
